hero.name: Kevin
hero.subtext: Yes, this entire website is actually for you.
hero.playfulSubtext: We considered sending a normal birthday message. Then someone suggested we over-engineer it.
hero.cardNote: From your colleagues & friends at Team Zenmonk

story.title: We could have just sent you a Slack message.
story.subtitle: But where's the fun in that?
paragraphs: When we thought about what to do for your birthday, we realized a standard message or corporate gift card would be painfully boring for our team.
So naturally, we spent engineering hours designing, animating, and deploying an entire digital experience to celebrate you.

photoSection.title: The Person Behind The CTO Title
photoSection.subtitle: Architectural debates, 'Why?' questions, and good coffee.

telemetryJoke.title: Team Observability Telemetry
telemetryJoke.punchline: You've taught us that 'it works on my machine' is not an architectural pattern and every simple endpoint deserves an aggregate design discussion. 😄

story.quote: “You're the person who makes us question our architecture, think in domain models, and genuinely love the craft.”

legacy.heading: THINGS WE SOMEHOW LEARNED ALONG THE WAY
legacy.subheading: A completely unbiased collection of things Kevin has convinced us to care about.
legacy.leadQuote: “Turns out good engineering isn't just making things work — it's having strong opinions on why it works.”

pillars.title: Domain-Driven Design
pillars.quote: “Apparently, 'just put it in the service' is not an architecture strategy.”
pillars.caption: We learned this one the hard way.
pillars.description: Listening to domain experts, keeping bounded contexts isolated, and realizing that an aggregate root isn't just a fancy folder.

pillars.title: Software Architecture
pillars.quote: “Turns out having folders called domain, application, and infrastructure doesn't automatically mean you have good architecture.”
pillars.caption: Kevin would probably like us to explain why in our next PR.
pillars.description: Structuring systems to isolate change, respecting boundaries, and thinking about what happens when requirements inevitably change.

pillars.title: System Design
pillars.quote: “'It works' and 'it's a good system' are apparently two completely different statements.”
pillars.caption: A classic Kevin code review insight.
pillars.description: Looking at asynchronous event streams, state lifecycles, scalability bottlenecks, and trade-offs before writing a single line of code.

pillars.title: Boundaries
pillars.quote: “Kevin has successfully convinced us that everything should not talk to everything else.”
pillars.caption: Coupling is the real enemy.
pillars.description: Understanding that just because you can import something doesn't mean you should. Explicit contracts and event-driven decoupled flow.

pillars.title: The Annoying Question
pillars.quote: “'Why?' — Somehow this one question has caused more architectural discussions than any framework ever has.”
pillars.caption: Challenging assumptions before implementing.
pillars.description: Digging into why a feature needs to be built that way, challenging assumptions, and avoiding unnecessary complexity.

seriousMoment.heading: But honestly...
seriousMoment.text1: Somewhere between the architecture debates, DDD discussions, system-design sessions, and all those 'quick' technical conversations...
seriousMoment.text2: You've pushed us to question our assumptions, understand the problem before jumping into code, and care about why we're building something — not just whether it works.
seriousMoment.closing: And that's something we genuinely appreciate.

legacy.transitionPause1: These stopped being random technical debates.
legacy.transitionPunchline: They became the way we build.
legacy.transitionNote: An engineering mindset forged in good humor and architectural rigor.

teamMessages.heading: THE PEOPLE WHO HAD TO LISTEN TO ALL OF THIS
teamMessages.subheading: A few words from the team.

paragraphs: From the very first architecture debate to every deep dive into domain modeling, working alongside you has completely transformed how we build systems. 😄
From DDD debates and system-design discussions to questioning why we built something the way we did — you've pushed us to think harder about what we're actually building.
A lot of the things we now consider normal engineering practice started as conversations with you.
We appreciate the trust, the freedom to experiment, the technical debates, and even those moments when our 'simple solution' turned out to need a little more thought.
Thanks for pushing us to become better engineers without making us feel like we're sitting in a classroom.
Happy Birthday, Kevin! Here's to another year of building things, learning things, and hopefully creating fewer production incidents. 🚀
chandanLetter.author: Chandan

members.name: Satvik
members.message: Happy Birthday Kevin! Thanks for constantly raising the engineering bar and showing us that 'it works on my machine' is not a valid architectural pattern. Hope you take a break from refactoring today!

members.name: Harish
members.message: Wishing you an awesome birthday, Kevin! May your coffee be strong, your tests all green, and your bounded contexts completely decoupled. Cheers!

members.name: Team Zenmonk
members.message: From debating domain event naming to fixing unexpected production quirks, we love working with you. Have the happiest birthday!

finalMessage.heading: BUT SERIOUSLY...
paragraphs: We're lucky to work with someone who makes us question our decisions, think a little deeper, and occasionally rethink an entire design five minutes before we thought we were done. 😄
You've helped us grow as engineers, but more importantly, you've made the journey interesting.
So here's to another year of building things, breaking things, arguing about architecture, fixing production, and figuring it out together.
finalMessage.closingLesson: “We're celebrating our CTO, teammate, and the guy who somehow got us all obsessed with architecture.”
finalMessage.signoff: From all of us at Team Zenmonk ❤️

celebration.subheading: Wishing you an extraordinary year filled with joy, great architecture, and great adventures.
